Swasth Setu app help
How to book an appointment:
- Open the Doctors tab, then search for a doctor or choose a specialty.
- Tap a doctor to see their details, then choose an available date and time slot.
- Confirm the booking. You get a token number for the appointment.
- You can see your upcoming appointments and token in the app after booking.
How to find a doctor:
- Use the search bar on the Doctors tab. You can type a doctor's name, a specialty, or your symptoms or illness in English, Hindi or Hinglish (for example "pet dard" or "chest pain").
title: Swasth Setu app help

text:
Swasth Setu app help
- Use the search bar on the Doctors tab. You can type a doctor's name, a specialty, or your symptoms or illness in English, Hindi or Hinglish (for example "pet dard" or "chest pain").
- The app understands the symptom and suggests the right type of doctor (specialization). If the symptoms look serious, an emergency banner is shown.
- You can also open the map to see doctors and hospitals near you.
How the SOS feature works:
- Shake your phone to trigger SOS in an emergency. You can also use the SOS button in the app.
title: Swasth Setu app help

text:
Swasth Setu app help
- Shake your phone to trigger SOS in an emergency. You can also use the SOS button in the app.
- SOS alerts the emergency contacts you saved. You choose these contacts from your phone book.
- The SOS screen also has helpline and police call buttons to call directly.
- Add your emergency contacts before you need them.
How the queue / token works:
- When you book an appointment at a hospital or clinic, you get a token number.
- The live queue shows which token is being served now and how many people are ahead of you, so you can estimate your waiting time without sitting in the waiting room.
title: Swasth Setu app help

- The live queue shows which token is being served now and how many people are ahead of you, so you can estimate your waiting time without sitting in the waiting room.

- Open Profile, then My Reports. Upload a text-based PDF report (PDF downloaded from the lab, not a photo or scan). Wait until the status shows ready, then ask the assistant about your report in the chat.

text:
First aid for burns and scalds
For a minor burn or scald, cool the burn as soon as possible under cool or lukewarm running water for about 20 minutes. Do not use ice, iced water or very cold water, as this can make the injury worse.
After cooling:
- Gently remove rings, watches or tight clothing near the burn before it swells, unless the clothing is stuck to the skin.
- Cover the burn loosely with cling film or a clean, non-fluffy cloth.
- Do not apply butter, oil, toothpaste, creams or home remedies. Do not burst blisters.
- Keep the person warm, but keep the burnt area uncovered by blankets.
title: First aid for burns and scalds

text:
First aid for burns and scalds
- Keep the person warm, but keep the burnt area uncovered by blankets.
Go to a hospital or call 108 or 112 for a burn that is large, deep or blistering, or on the face, hands, feet, genitals or a joint. Also get urgent help for burns in babies, children, older people or pregnant women, burns caused by chemicals or electricity, burns from fire with smoke inhalation, or if the person has trouble breathing.
title: First aid for burns and scalds

text:
First aid for cuts and bleeding
To stop bleeding, press firmly on the wound with a clean cloth or bandage. Keep pressing without lifting the cloth to check. If the injury is on an arm or leg, raise it above the level of the heart if possible, and have the person sit or lie down.
For a small cut or graze, wash your hands, rinse the wound under clean running water, pat the area dry and cover it with a clean dressing. Change the dressing if it gets wet or dirty.
title: First aid for cuts and bleeding

text:
First aid for cuts and bleeding
For a small cut or graze, wash your hands, rinse the wound under clean running water, pat the area dry and cover it with a clean dressing. Change the dressing if it gets wet or dirty.
Get urgent medical help or call 108 or 112 if the bleeding is heavy, spurts out, or does not stop after 10 minutes of firm pressure. Do not remove an object that is stuck in a wound; press around it and get help.
title: First aid for cuts and bleeding

text:
First aid for cuts and bleeding
See a doctor for a cut that is deep, wide or gaping, is very dirty, was caused by an animal or human bite, or is on the face. Also see a doctor if the wound becomes red, swollen, warm, painful or leaks pus, or if you have fever. Ask a doctor whether you need a tetanus shot after a dirty or deep wound.
title: First aid for cuts and bleeding

text:
Dehydration and oral rehydration solution (ORS)
Dehydration happens when the body loses more water and salts than it takes in. It is common with diarrhoea, vomiting, fever and hot weather, and it is most dangerous in babies, young children and older people.
Common signs of dehydration are thirst, a dry mouth, dark yellow urine or passing urine less often, tiredness and dizziness. In children, look for sunken eyes, restlessness or irritability, drinking eagerly, and being unusually sleepy.
title: Dehydration and oral rehydration solution (ORS)

text:
Dehydration and oral rehydration solution (ORS)
ORS (oral rehydration solution) is a mixture of clean water, sugar and salt. It replaces the water and salts lost from the body. ORS packets are sold at pharmacies and are available at many health centres.
How to use ORS:
- Mix the packet exactly as the instructions on the packet say, using clean water. Do not add extra salt or sugar.
- Give small sips often, especially if there is vomiting. Keep going even if the person vomits once.
- Keep feeding children and keep breastfeeding babies during diarrhoea.
title: Dehydration and oral rehydration solution (ORS)

text:
Dehydration and oral rehydration solution (ORS)
- Keep feeding children and keep breastfeeding babies during diarrhoea.
Get medical help if there is blood in the stool, the person cannot drink or keeps vomiting, is very sleepy or limp, passes no urine for many hours, has sunken eyes, or if the diarrhoea does not improve after a couple of days.
title: Dehydration and oral rehydration solution (ORS)

text:
Diabetes basics
Diabetes is a lifelong condition in which there is too much sugar (glucose) in the blood. The body either does not make enough insulin or cannot use it properly. The main types are type 1, type 2 and gestational diabetes, which can appear during pregnancy.
Common symptoms are feeling very thirsty, passing urine more often, feeling tired, losing weight without trying, blurred vision, cuts or wounds that heal slowly, and frequent infections. Some people with type 2 diabetes have no symptoms for years, so testing is important if you are at risk.
title: Diabetes basics

text:
Diabetes basics
Only a doctor can diagnose diabetes, using blood tests. Anyone with these symptoms, or with a family history of diabetes, should see a doctor for a check.
Healthy habits that help prevent type 2 diabetes or keep it under control:
- Eat a balanced diet with less sugar, sweets and fried food.
- Stay active and keep a healthy weight.
- Avoid tobacco.
- Go for regular check-ups, including eye, foot and kidney checks if you have diabetes.
Get urgent medical help if a person with diabetes becomes very drowsy or confused, vomits repeatedly, breathes deeply and fast, or has breath that smells fruity.
title: Diabetes basics

text:
Fever in adults
A fever means your body temperature is higher than normal, usually around 38°C or above. It is often a sign that the body is fighting an infection such as a cold or flu. Many fevers get better on their own within a few days.
Things that can help at home:
- Rest as much as you can.
- Drink plenty of fluids, ideally water, so that your urine stays light yellow and clear.
- Wear light clothing and keep the room comfortably cool.
- Stay at home and avoid mixing with other people while you have a fever.
title: Fever in adults

text:
Fever in adults
- Stay at home and avoid mixing with other people while you have a fever.
See a doctor soon if the fever does not improve after a few days, keeps coming back, or gets worse despite home care. Get medical help the same day if you also have a stiff neck, a rash that does not fade, trouble breathing, chest pain, confusion, repeated vomiting, a seizure, or if you cannot keep fluids down.
Older people, pregnant women and people with long-term illnesses such as diabetes, heart disease or kidney disease should see a doctor sooner. Ask a doctor or pharmacist before taking any medicine.
title: Fever in adults

text:
Fever in children and babies
Fever is common in children and is usually caused by a viral infection. Most children with a fever recover at home, but babies and young children need extra care because they can become unwell quickly.
A baby younger than 3 months with a fever of 38°C or above should be seen by a doctor urgently, even if the baby looks well.
Care at home for older babies and children:
- Offer plenty of fluids. Keep breastfeeding or bottle feeding as usual.
- Dress the child in light clothing. Do not wrap a child up warmly and do not sponge with cold water.
title: Fever in children and babies

text:
Fever in children and babies
- Dress the child in light clothing. Do not wrap a child up warmly and do not sponge with cold water.
- Watch the child closely and keep checking on them, including during the night.
Get urgent medical help if the child is very sleepy or hard to wake, is floppy, is breathing fast or with difficulty, has a rash that does not fade, has a stiff neck, has a seizure, is not drinking or has not passed urine for many hours, or has cold hands and feet along with the fever. Ask a doctor or pharmacist before giving any medicine to a child.
title: Fever in children and babies

text:
Suspected broken bone or sprain
A broken bone (fracture) may cause severe pain, swelling, bruising, a bent or odd shape, or being unable to move or put weight on the injured part. A sprain is an injury to the ligaments around a joint and can look similar.
If you think a bone may be broken:
- Keep the injured part as still as possible. Do not try to straighten it or push a bone back in.
- Support the area with a sling, a folded cloth or by resting it on a cushion.
- Wrap an ice pack or cold pack in a cloth and hold it on the area to reduce swelling. Do not put ice directly on the skin.
title: Suspected broken bone or sprain

text:
Suspected broken bone or sprain
- Wrap an ice pack or cold pack in a cloth and hold it on the area to reduce swelling. Do not put ice directly on the skin.
- Do not eat or drink anything in case an operation is needed.
- Go to a hospital emergency department.
Call 108 or 112 if the injury is from a serious fall or accident, if a bone is sticking out through the skin, if there is heavy bleeding, if the neck or back may be injured, or if the person is pale, faint or very unwell. Do not move a person with a suspected neck or back injury unless they are in danger.
title: Suspected broken bone or sprain

text:
Healthy daily habits
Small daily habits protect health over the long term and lower the risk of heart disease, diabetes, high blood pressure and some cancers.
Be active: adults are advised to do at least 150 minutes of moderate physical activity such as brisk walking every week, spread across the week, and to move more and sit less during the day.
Eat well: choose fruit, vegetables, pulses and whole grains. Limit salt, sugar and fried or packaged foods. Drink enough clean water through the day.
title: Healthy daily habits

text:
Healthy daily habits
Eat well: choose fruit, vegetables, pulses and whole grains. Limit salt, sugar and fried or packaged foods. Drink enough clean water through the day.
Sleep and mind: most adults need about 7 to 9 hours of sleep. Take breaks, spend time with family and friends, and talk to someone or see a doctor if you feel low or anxious for a long time.
Avoid harm: do not use tobacco in any form and limit alcohol.
title: Healthy daily habits

text:
Healthy daily habits
Avoid harm: do not use tobacco in any form and limit alcohol.
Prevention: wash your hands with soap, keep vaccinations up to date, and get regular health check-ups, especially if you are over 40 or have a family history of diabetes, high blood pressure or heart disease.
title: Healthy daily habits

text:
High blood pressure (hypertension)
High blood pressure means the force of blood against the walls of your arteries stays higher than it should be. Over time it increases the risk of heart attack, stroke and kidney problems.
Most people with high blood pressure have no symptoms, so the only way to know is to have it measured. A doctor decides whether blood pressure is high, usually after repeated readings. Adults should get their blood pressure checked regularly, especially if they are older, overweight or have a family history of high blood pressure, diabetes or heart disease.
title: High blood pressure (hypertension)

text:
High blood pressure (hypertension)
Lifestyle habits that help keep blood pressure healthy:
- Eat less salt and fewer processed and fried foods. Eat more fruit, vegetables and whole grains.
- Be physically active on most days.
- Keep a healthy weight.
- Avoid tobacco and limit alcohol.
- Sleep well and find ways to reduce stress.
People who have been prescribed treatment should keep following their doctor's advice and not stop on their own. Get emergency help for a sudden severe headache, chest pain, trouble breathing, vision problems, weakness on one side of the body or confusion.
title: High blood pressure (hypertension)

text:
Safe water, food and hand hygiene
Many stomach infections, including diarrhoea, spread through dirty water, unsafe food and unwashed hands. They can be prevented with a few simple steps.
- Wash your hands with soap and water after using the toilet, after cleaning a child, before cooking and before eating.
- Drink safe water. If you are not sure the water is clean, boil it and let it cool, or use a safe filter.
- Wash fruit and vegetables well, and cook food thoroughly. Keep raw and cooked food apart and eat freshly cooked food.
- Keep food covered and stored properly, and keep kitchens and toilets clean.
title: Safe water, food and hand hygiene

text:
Safe water, food and hand hygiene
- Keep food covered and stored properly, and keep kitchens and toilets clean.
- Use clean toilets and dispose of waste safely.
If someone in the family has diarrhoea or vomiting, wash hands often, keep their utensils clean and make sure they drink plenty of fluids, including ORS. See a doctor if there is blood in the stool or signs of dehydration.
title: Safe water, food and hand hygiene

text:
Stomach pain (abdominal pain)
Mild stomach pain is common and often settles by itself. Causes include indigestion, gas, constipation, food that did not agree with you, and stomach infections. It can also be a sign of something more serious, so the pattern of the pain matters.
What may help with mild pain at home:
- Rest and drink small sips of water or clear fluids.
- Eat light, plain food once you feel able to, and avoid very oily, spicy or heavy meals.
- Notice when the pain started, where it is, and whether it comes with fever, vomiting or diarrhoea.
title: Stomach pain (abdominal pain)

text:
Stomach pain (abdominal pain)
- Notice when the pain started, where it is, and whether it comes with fever, vomiting or diarrhoea.
See a doctor if the pain lasts more than a few days, keeps coming back, or comes with weight loss, a swollen belly or changes in bowel habits. A general physician is a good first doctor to see. A gastroenterologist treats stomach and digestive problems.
title: Stomach pain (abdominal pain)

text:
Stomach pain (abdominal pain)
Get urgent medical help if the pain is sudden and severe, the belly is hard or very tender, there is vomiting blood, black or bloody stools, a high fever, yellow skin or eyes, trouble breathing, or if the pain happens in pregnancy. Pain with sweating, breathlessness or chest pressure can be a heart problem and is an emergency.
title: Stomach pain (abdominal pain)

text:
When to call 108 or 112 and go to an emergency department
In India you can call 112 (national emergency number) or 108 (ambulance) for medical emergencies. Do not wait or try home remedies if someone has any of these signs.
Call for emergency help right away for:
- Chest pain, pressure or tightness, especially with sweating, breathlessness or pain spreading to the arm, jaw or back.
- Trouble breathing or being unable to speak in full sentences.
- Signs of a stroke: face drooping on one side, weakness or numbness in an arm or leg, slurred speech or sudden confusion. Note the time the signs started.
title: When to call 108 or 112 and go to an emergency department

text:
When to call 108 or 112 and go to an emergency department
- Signs of a stroke: face drooping on one side, weakness or numbness in an arm or leg, slurred speech or sudden confusion. Note the time the signs started.
- Loss of consciousness, fainting that does not recover quickly, or a seizure.
- Heavy bleeding that does not stop with firm pressure.
- A severe allergic reaction with swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing.
- Suspected poisoning or overdose.
- Severe burns, a serious accident or head injury, especially with vomiting or drowsiness.
- Sudden severe headache, or sudden severe pain anywhere.
title: When to call 108 or 112 and go to an emergency department

text:
When to call 108 or 112 and go to an emergency department
- Sudden severe headache, or sudden severe pain anywhere.
While waiting for help, stay calm, keep the person still and comfortable, and do not give food or drink. If the person is not breathing, start CPR if you know how. You can also use the SOS feature in this app.
title: When to call 108 or 112 and go to an emergency department
